title: Kin to the divine
hook: if we're kin to the divine, why think meanly of ourselves? (Discourses 1.3, 1.9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Helvidius Priscus, and the purple thread, the narrow bright stripe in a plain cloak. Did you get to be that thread anywhere? Day three hundred ninety-three.

A letter arrives: the emperor has adopted you. Overnight you're family to the man who rules the world. If that happened, Epictetus jokes, no one could stand your pride. Then he turns the joke around. His students had been taught something much bigger than that letter: that they were kin to God. So why, he asks, do they go around thinking so little of themselves? Today: kin to the divine.
screen: `ADOPTED BY THE EMPEROR.` → `YOU'D WALK DIFFERENTLY.` → `SOMETHING BIGGER THAN THAT.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter three. For the Stoics, God is the reason running through the whole universe, and every human carries a share of it: our own reason. That's the kinship. Epictetus says we're made of two things mixed together. A body, which we share with the animals. And reason and judgment, which we share with the gods. Many, he says, lean toward the first. And then he gets specific, the way he does. Some of us become like wolves, faithless and treacherous. Some like lions, wild and cruel. Most of us, he says, end up as foxes: small, sly, getting away with things. None of that is what we're made for. Chapter nine pushes it further. Ask Socrates where he's from, Epictetus says, and he wouldn't answer Athens. He'd say: from the world. If you're kin to the reason that runs everything, you belong to all of it, not just to one town. Other traditions have their own way of saying something nearby. Genesis says, in the King James words, "So God created man in his own image." Jews and Christians read that their own way, and the Stoic idea is its own thing, built on reason. But both refuse to let a person think of themselves as small stuff. Epictetus isn't flattering anyone. Kinship is a standard, not a compliment. If you're family, act like it. Not by bragging about the family name, but by living the way the family lives: fair, clear-headed, and not easily frightened.
screen: `TWO THINGS MIXED: BODY AND REASON.` · `WOLVES, LIONS, FOXES.` · `SOCRATES: FROM THE WORLD.` · `KINSHIP IS A STANDARD.` · then, large: `KIN.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand, and let your spine come up tall, not stiff, just tall. Feel the crown of your head lift a little. Let the shoulders drop. Breathe. Now notice where you usually shrink: a meeting, a phone call, a relative's kitchen. Picture yourself there, sitting this tall. Not proud, not loud. Just someone who remembers what they're made of. The bell holds the time.
Kin to the divine. The Stoic idea that our reason is a share of the reason that runs the world, so no one should think meanly of themselves.
Your line: kin. The next time you feel yourself shrinking or turning foxy, stand up straight and remember the family you belong to. Day three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often recall Epictetus' kinship argument when they catch themselves acting from fear or pettiness, and some simply straighten their posture as a physical reminder.

original.note: Greek syngeneia: kinship, being of one family; Epictetus uses it for our relation to God.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone is special.
what it means: our reason is a share of the reason that runs the world, so we're held to that standard.
what a scholar hears: Stoic theology made God the rational fire running through the cosmos, so 'kinship' is literal for them: a fragment of the same reason in each person.
